opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the gap between what's actually written in natural text and what the model needs to see to execute an algorithm reliably.

When people write about addition, or when you see arithmetic on the internet, the reasoning is almost always compressed. Somebody writes "27 plus 48 is 75" and that's it. All the intermediate work, lining up the digits, adding the ones place, noticing you get 15, writing the 5 and carrying the 1, happens in their head or on scratch paper that never gets written down. So the model gets lots of input-output pairs but very little of the procedure that connects them.

And these models are excellent at picking up patterns, but if the procedure is underspecified they'll pick up whatever pattern fits the data they've seen, and that's often a shortcut. It might work for two- or three-digit numbers and then fall apart as soon as you go longer, because it never learned the general rule. It learned something that happened to correlate with the right answers in the range it saw.

That was the main motivation behind our work on algorithmic prompting. We found that if you want the model to really follow the algorithm, you have to spell out every step with no ambiguity. Even standard chain-of-thought prompts leave a lot implicit. They might say "add the digits and carry over," but they don't say which digit is being indexed, what the carry value is right now, or how that carry feeds into the next step. Each of those gaps gives the model room to improvise, and improvising is exactly what you don't want when you're executing a procedure.

So when we wrote out the explanations in painstaking detail, tracking each digit, stating the carry explicitly, and repeating the same structure at every step, the model's ability to generalize to much longer problems than it saw in the prompt improved a lot. That suggests the capability is there in some sense. The model can follow a procedure in context. It just needs the procedure to be fully specified, because it can't reliably infer the unstated parts.

There's a broader lesson here too, I think. A lot of what looks like reasoning failure in these models may really be a specification problem. We, as humans, are used to communicating with other humans who share an enormous amount of implicit context. When we teach a child addition, we also rely on a lot of shared intuition. The model doesn't necessarily share that, so the more explicit you are, the less it has to guess.

r001.rationale: The response explains that people assume shared context and that a model cannot reliably infer unstated procedural details, so apparently obvious addition instructions may be interpreted through shortcuts or improvisation.

r002.rationale: It says underspecified procedures can lead to shortcuts, but does not explain that carry values in a limited set of examples are consistent with multiple rules for deriving them.

r003.rationale: It reports that detailed demonstrations improved generalization to much longer addition problems than those shown in the prompt.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to what the model actually has to learn. When we give a model a bunch of addition problems with just the final answer, we're asking it to infer a procedure from input-output pairs, and that's a surprisingly hard inference problem. Addition on long numbers involves carrying, it involves aligning digits by position, and none of that structure is visible in the answer alone. So the model ends up finding shortcuts, things like memorizing patterns for common digit combinations or approximating the result statistically, and those shortcuts fall apart the moment you move to longer numbers than it saw in training.

What we found in the algorithmic prompting work is that if you spell out every step, really every step, including the parts a human would consider too obvious to say, the model does something quite different. You tell it: take the rightmost digit of each number, add them, write down the ones digit, note whether there's a carry, move left, and so on. And crucially you show that reasoning unrolled, with the intermediate state written out explicitly, so the model never has to hold anything implicitly in its head.

The reason the explicitness matters so much is that language models are very good at pattern-matching on text, and if there's any ambiguity in the demonstration, they'll fill in the gap with whatever prior they have, which is usually the shortcut. Leaving out a step, or saying "and then carry the one" without actually showing where the one goes, creates room for the model to improvise, and it tends to improvise wrong. So the demonstrations have to be almost tediously unambiguous. It's a bit like writing instructions for someone who will follow them literally and has no common sense about arithmetic at all.

The encouraging part is that when you do it that way, you see real length generalization. The model can handle numbers far longer than anything in the prompt, because it's genuinely executing the procedure rather than guessing the result. And to me that was the interesting finding, that these models can run algorithms in context, but you have to teach them the way you'd teach a computer, not the way you'd teach a person.

r001.rationale: The response says that when instructions leave steps implicit, the model fills gaps using its learned priors and shortcuts, showing why expecting it to infer seemingly obvious addition steps is a faulty assumption.

r002.rationale: It discusses shortcuts and ambiguity generally, but does not say that carry values in a limited set of examples could fit multiple rules for deriving them.

r003.rationale: It reports length generalization to numbers beyond those in the prompt and says the model applies the spelled-out procedure rather than guessing.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the difficulty is that getting the right answer and learning the algorithm are different things. A model can pick up patterns that work for the examples it sees without learning a procedure that generalizes to longer numbers.

With addition, we tend to take the intermediate steps for granted: align the digits, start from the right, add each column, and carry when necessary. But if you only show the model a question and an answer, those steps are hidden. Explicit demonstrations make the procedure visible, including how a carry affects the next column.

So I wouldn’t necessarily say that a language model can only learn addition this way. It’s more that explicit demonstrations help distinguish the algorithm we want it to learn from other patterns that happen to fit the training examples.

r001.rationale: The response says the addition steps may be hidden when only answers are shown, but it does not identify an assumption about the model’s interpretive biases in expecting it to understand seemingly obvious instructions.

r002.rationale: It mentions carrying, but does not explain that carry values in a limited set of examples could fit multiple rules for deriving them.

r003.rationale: It says explicit demonstrations make the procedure visible and help the model learn an algorithm that generalizes to longer numbers, communicating flexible application to new situations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the difficulty is that getting the right answer doesn’t necessarily require learning the algorithm. If you train on lots of short addition problems, the model can pick up patterns that work on those examples without learning a procedure that generalizes to longer numbers.

The addition algorithm has a very particular structure: you work column by column, keep track of a carry, and repeat the same operation. That structure is obvious to us because we’ve been taught it, but it isn’t explicit in a question-and-answer pair. Demonstrating the intermediate steps makes the procedure visible and gives the model a much stronger signal about what it should learn.

So I wouldn’t necessarily say explicit demonstrations are the only way a model could learn addition. They help distinguish learning a reusable algorithm from learning patterns that happen to produce correct answers on the training distribution.

r001.rationale: The response says the algorithm seems obvious to people who have been taught it, but does not identify an assumption about the model’s interpretive biases when given seemingly obvious instructions.

r002.rationale: It mentions tracking a carry, but does not explain that the carry values in a limited set of examples could fit multiple derivation rules.

r003.rationale: It says intermediate-step demonstrations provide a stronger signal for learning a reusable algorithm that generalizes to longer numbers and new examples.
